svg.aria-label: Diagram of how CVE-2026-89049 turns a port-forwarding permission into portable credentials. A user holding ssm:StartSession opens a remote-host port forwarding session through SSM Agent. The agent holds a denylist of forbidden remote destinations intended to block link-local addresses, but the comparison is made against the literal spelling, so an equivalent representation of the same address is not matched and passes. The forwarded connection therefore terminates on the instance metadata service at the link-local address, reached from the instance's own network stack. The temporary IAM role credentials returned are ordinary credentials with no binding to the instance, so they can be used from anywhere. A second panel lists the IMDSv2 protections — the session token is bound to the instance that generated it, PUT requests carrying an X-Forwarded-For header are rejected, and the PUT response hop limit defaults to one — and notes that all three target a request arriving from outside the instance through a proxy, not one that terminates on the instance itself.
svg.title: The denylist compared a spelling, not an address
svg.text: A permission to forward a port became a permission to take the role
CVE-2026-89049 · SSM Agent below 3.3.4851.0 · fixed in 3.3.4851.0
1 · Authenticated user
ssm:StartSession
remote-host port forwarding
2 · The denylist
Compares the literal spelling.
An equivalent form passes.
3 · Link-local reached
4 · Credentials
The instance role’s,
usable off-instance.
What IMDSv2 defends against
• PUT with an X-Forwarded-For header is rejected
• PUT response hop limit defaults to 1
• The token is instance-specific and “will be rejected
if you attempt to use it outside of the instance on
which it was generated”
All three assume the request comes from outside.
Why it does not stop this
The session terminates on the instance, so the
onward request comes from its own network stack.
Hop limit satisfied. No forwarding header. Token
generated where it is valid.
The binding is on the token. The credentials it
returns are bound to nothing.
Two speeds of response
Today, centrally, no instance access needed: scope ssm:StartSession so untrusted principals cannot use AWS-StartPortForwardingSessionToRemoteHost.
Then everywhere, with a tail: upgrade SSM Agent past 3.3.4851.0 — starting with the instances whose profiles carry the broadest permissions.
The root cause is a class, not a bug. A denylist has to enumerate every spelling of a forbidden thing, and the attacker picks the spelling — the same
failure as the “incomplete list of disallowed inputs” that broke read-only mode in post #26.
